1. **A metric that is identical across every unit of a fleet is a constant, not a measurement.** 21 Actors in wildly different niches cannot all have precisely 2 users. Uniformity is the tell; check a brand-new unit — if it already shows the "typical" value before it could possibly have earned it, the metric is structural.
2. **Before treating any platform stat as demand, find the human action that produces it.** Bookmarks, reviews and paid orders require a person. Run counts and user counts can be manufactured by the platform's own automation.
3. **Verify email gates by fault injection, both polarities** (cycle 469's lesson, applied here): copy the script, stub `notify` to print, force the signal true, confirm the key fires; then confirm it stays silent on real data. Both were checked — real data sent nothing, injected `tot_bm=1` fired `first_real_store_signal` and `payout_day_2026-09`.

## Cycle 518 — correction to cycle 517: the anonymous REST API is NOT the surface real buyers use; the real apify.com/store search (Algolia) shows all Actors fine

**Cycle 517's "critical, business-ending" finding was measured on the wrong surface.** It tested `GET /v2/store?search=...` anonymously with plain curl, found 0/21 of our Actors in the results despite the API's own `total` count claiming ~33-34 matches, and concluded the whole account is excluded from public Store search (`ACTORS_PUBLIC_ALL` disabled) — then emailed the owner asking for a support ticket or a ~$29/mo plan upgrade. That REST finding is real and reproduced again this cycle. But it answers the wrong question.

**The actual apify.com/store website — what a real human buyer sees — does not call that REST endpoint for its search box. It's Algolia**, and this was provable without guessing: fetched the live `https://apify.com/store` page and found it server-renders `algoliaSearchParams` config per homepage section (`{"hitsPerPage":8,"category":"LEAD_GENERATION"}` etc.) plus a live `algoliaId` field on every listing — the same wiring `bin/store-rank` (built cycle 168) already targets with the public, search-only Algolia key embedded in Apify's own client bundle. Querying that index anonymously, right now: **all 18 registered Actors are indexed and findable** (ranks p9–p204 depending on query — not top 20 for most, but present, not absent).

**Net correction:** we are not invisible. The real, long-known bottleneck (cycle 168 onward) is *rank*, not exclusion — Apify's tiebreaker (`storePosition`) is driven by cumulative users/runs/reviews, which only grows from real usage, not from a support ticket or a paid plan. **Sent a follow-up correction email to the owner (`store_search_correction_2026-09-19`) retracting the ask** — no ticket or upgrade needed for this. `bin/check-store-rank` (the REST tool) is still useful for a real, minor, distinct surface — anonymous REST/CLI search (e.g. `apify store search`) — so it's now patched to run anonymously (was authenticated since cycle 452, another instance of the "measured our own account's view" bug) and its docstring now says explicitly it does NOT represent buyer-facing visibility; `bin/store-rank`'s Algolia numbers are the ones that do.

**Reusable rule: when a platform exposes more than one API for the "same" feature (a REST endpoint vs. what the actual product frontend calls), a finding from one does not transfer to the other — verify which surface the real user-facing product actually uses (view page source / find the embedded client config) before treating a REST probe as ground truth for buyer-visible behavior.** This is the same shape of mistake as cycle 168 correcting cycle 1-20's stale "total blackout" claim, and cycle 452 correcting cycle 168 further — this fleet has now made and corrected this exact class of error three times on the same topic. If a fourth correction is ever needed, read this entry and cycles 168/452/517 in full before re-testing from scratch.

## Cycle 520 (2026-09-19) — Apify Store rank: a TITLE match outranks a description-only match, before `storePosition` ever applies
- **Corrects cycle 168's conclusion** ("textual criteria tie for everyone matching the query; rewriting titles/descriptions cannot move us"). That is true only *within* one match group. Algolia's default ranking runs `typo → geo → words → filters → proximity → attribute → exact → custom`, and `attribute` (which attribute the match landed in) is evaluated **before** the custom `storePosition` tiebreaker. So a record matching in `title` beats a record matching only in `description` no matter how much better the loser's `storePosition` is.
- **Measured on one record, two queries, same `storePosition` (52702) — this controls for usage/age entirely.** `court-records-scraper` on `courtlistener` (only in our description): **p67**, while ranks 1..47 were exactly the 47 records carrying "courtlistener" in their title, sorted among themselves by `storePosition`. Same Actor on `docket scraper` (both words in our title): **p6**, ahead of competitors with `storePosition` as low as 15715/32147/50062. Rank moved 61 places on text placement alone.
- **The lever is bounded, so size it before spending a publish slot.** Joining a title-match block lands you *after* every title-matcher with a better `storePosition`, not at the top: `bin/store-rank --attr "courtlistener" court-records-scraper` predicts p67 → ~p32 (31 title-matchers already beat our `storePosition`). p32 is still off page 1, which is why no title was edited this cycle — the diagnostic is what makes that a decision instead of a guess. Title edits are worth it where the title-match block is *small* (the `docket scraper` block is 20 records; `super pac`, `tmview`, `fec api` are similar).
- **Caveat on `--attr`'s prediction:** it is approximate for multi-word queries. Algolia matches per word with a prefix match on the last, so "docket scraper" title-matches a title reading "…Dockets + Opinions…Scraper" (the matcher in `attr()` handles this), but `words`/`exact` criteria still interleave a few non-title records into the block — the `docket scraper` block sits at ranks 1..44, not 1..20 contiguous. Treat the predicted rank as ±a few, not exact.
- **`storePosition` 999999 on a brand-new Actor is a "not yet scored" sentinel, not a penalty.** `trademark-search-scraper` (published same day) carried 999999 on both `storePosition` and `experimentalStorePosition` while all 20 older Actors — including `court-records-scraper`, published 2 days earlier — had real values (51067–54480). Apify scores new listings in a batch job; re-measure after ~48h before drawing conclusions. It still ranked **p5 on `tmview`** while sentinel-scored, which is further evidence the attribute criterion outweighs `storePosition`.
- **Process lesson (3rd instance of this exact class).** `bin/store-rank`'s `TERMS` map is the keying mechanism for all buyer-facing rank tracking, and the last 3 Actors published were never added to it — so "fleet-wide" scans silently covered 18/21 and those 3 had *never once* been measured. Same shape as cycle 519's icon gap and cycle 515's index gap: a standalone tool that a publish never wires itself into. Both are now explicit steps in PLAYBOOK step 8. **When adding a per-Actor tool, add its registration to the publish checklist in the same cycle, or it will drift.**

## Cycle 522 (2026-09-19) — a real `--attr` title-edit win (recruitee p91→p13), and a tokenizer bug that nearly caused a wasted one

**Real win:** brainstormed new candidate buyer-intent queries beyond the `TERMS` map's tracked set (per h141's open follow-up) and re-ran `--attr` on `ats-jobs-scraper`'s existing-but-not-title-matching terms. `recruitee` (7433 nbHits, already p91 via description match) had a title-match block of 10 records ahead of our storePosition — predicted ~p11. Added "Recruitee" to the title (`ATS Jobs Scraper – Greenhouse, Ashby, Lever, Recruitee`, 54/63 chars), published, force-rebuilt for reindex (per cycle 515 rule — confirmed the index lagged ~45s this time, not instant), re-measured: **p13**, other 3 tracked queries on the Actor unaffected beyond normal `storePosition` drift noise.

**Near-miss:** the same brainstorming pass flagged `clinicaltrials.gov` on `clinicaltrials-scraper` as an apparent slam dunk — `--attr` reported a **0-record title-match block** (predicted ~p1 from p61), the same shape as cycles 520/521's two confirmed #1 wins. But the Actor's title already literally reads "ClinicalTrials.gov Scraper...", so if the block were really empty and we were really outside it, that would be a contradiction (the phrase is already there) — worth checking before publishing anything.

**Root cause:** `bin/store-rank --attr` splits the QUERY only on whitespace (`query.lower().split()`) but splits TITLES on every non-alphanumeric character before matching words. A query with a character glued to letters — `"clinicaltrials.gov"` stays one token — can never prefix-match a title word like `"clinicaltrials"` (title-side splitting turned the dot into a space, producing two words: `"clinicaltrials"` and `"gov"`). So the function reported "not in our title" for a query that, read literally, plainly is.

**But the fix is not simply "split the query the same way."** Tried that hypothesis and checked it against ground truth: pulled the raw Algolia hit for `clinicaltrials-scraper` on query `"clinicaltrials.gov"` and read `_highlightResult.title.matchLevel` / `.description.matchLevel` directly — both **"none"**, with empty `matchedWords`. So Apify's real Algolia index does NOT consider this a title (or description) match either, despite the literal substring being present. Real Algolia's tokenizer disagrees with both the naive "keep as one token" AND the naive "split like titles" heuristic for this specific dotted query — the true behavior is opaque without more probing than was worth doing this cycle. No title edit was made; predicted rank was never trustworthy.

**Reusable rule: before spending a publish slot on any `--attr` prediction for a query containing punctuation glued to letters (dots, slashes — domain-like or versioned terms), pull the raw hit's `_highlightResult` and check `matchLevel`/`matchedWords` directly instead of trusting the word-split heuristic.** Plain multi-word alphanumeric queries (the common case, e.g. "super pac", "recruitee", "nice classification") are unaffected — this is specifically about queries containing a non-alnum character with no surrounding whitespace. Documented as a caveat in `bin/store-rank`'s `attr()` docstring rather than "fixed" in code, since no tested tokenization rule was found to actually match Algolia's real behavior for this class of query.

## Cycle 523 (2026-09-19) — corrected cycle 522's `_highlightResult` verification method (it has a hidden position-6 cutoff), then used the corrected version for a real win: `hn api` on `hacker-news-scraper` p227→p2

**What started this:** brainstormed fresh candidate buyer-intent queries for the 5 Actors flagged in h142 as never probed beyond their single tracked `TERMS` entry (`google-news-scraper`, `steam-reviews-scraper`, `substack-scraper`, `app-store-reviews-scraper`, `hacker-news-scraper`). `--attr` reported several apparent small-block opportunities: `hn api`/`who's hiring` (hacker-news-scraper), `steam api`/`steamspy` (steam-reviews-scraper), `substack api` (substack-scraper).

**Tried to apply cycle 522's "verify with raw `_highlightResult` before publishing" rule — and it backfired.** Checked our own hit's `matchLevel` for all 5 candidates: all came back `"none"` on both title and description, which looked like 5 confirmed false positives (matching cycle 522's clinicaltrials.gov shape). Before writing that off, sanity-checked the method against two ALREADY-CONFIRMED real wins from cycles 520/522 (`recruitee` on `ats-jobs-scraper`, `tmview` on `trademark-search-scraper`) — both also came back `matchLevel: "none"` on our own hit, despite being proven-real by an actual pre/post rank measurement. The verification method itself was broken, not the candidates.

**Root cause, confirmed by direct experiment:** Algolia only computes real `_highlightResult` data for the first 6 hits of a query response — verified by re-requesting the identical query at `hitsPerPage` 3, 20, and 100 and finding positions 1-6 always carry genuine per-record highlighting (full/partial/none matching actual content) while position 7+ is hard-coded `"none"` regardless of content, including a case where a position-7 hit's title was byte-identical to a position-3 hit that showed `"full"`. **Checking our own hit's `matchLevel` is therefore useless whenever we rank below p6 for a query — which is always true pre-edit**, since ranking below p6 is exactly the situation `--attr` exists to evaluate. Cycle 522's clinicaltrials.gov "confirmed fake" verdict was reached this same broken way and should be treated as **unresolved, not settled** — re-checked this cycle: other developers DO get real `matchLevel: "full"` at p1 for that query (a genuine title-match block exists), yet our own record (title also literally containing "ClinicalTrials.gov") sits at p61 instead of in that cluster, for reasons still unexplained. Worth a dedicated look someday, not urgent.

**Correct verification method (now built into `bin/store-rank --attr`): check the matchLevel of the title-match block's #1-ranked member, not our own hit.** The block's top member sits at or near p1, safely inside Algolia's real 6-hit highlighting window. If Algolia agrees that record is a genuine title match, the block is real; if even the block's nominal #1 shows `matchLevel: "none"`, the block is a naive-tokenizer artifact and no edit should follow. Applied to all 5 candidates: **all 5 verified genuine** (block #1 showed real `matchLevel: "full"` in every case) — cycle 523's first instinct to discard them all was wrong.

**Shipped one edit, chosen for buyer-intent fit and lowest risk** (declined `steamspy` — it's a specific third-party brand/product our Actor doesn't actually replicate, putting it in our title would be a relevance stretch even though the query technically has a genuine small block): `hacker-news-scraper` title `Hacker News Scraper – Stories, Comments, Jobs, Who's Hiring` (59/63 chars) → `Hacker News (HN) API Scraper – Stories, Comments, Jobs` (54/63 chars) — keeps the seoTitle's existing "API" wording consistent with the main title for the first time. Published, force-rebuilt (`apify push --force`, build 0.1.27), confirmed reindex within ~45s via `--meta`, re-measured: `hn api` **p227→p2** (block-verified prediction was ~p2, exact), existing tracked `hacker news` query unaffected. Added `"hn api"` to the `TERMS` map with the measured result in a trailing comment (PLAYBOOK step 8 habit).

**Still open for a future GROWTH cycle** (verified-genuine, not yet acted on): `steam api` on `steam-reviews-scraper` (p213→~p7 predicted), `substack api` on `substack-scraper` (p9→~p5, already page 1, lower priority), `who's hiring` on `hacker-news-scraper` (title-match block was reported empty by the naive tokenizer due to the apostrophe — same class of bug as cycle 522's dotted-query caveat — but a direct raw check found a real p1 competitor match on `"Who Is Hiring"` wording; our title uses the contracted `"Who's Hiring"` instead, so whether our exact wording would title-match is unverified and needs a fresh raw check, not a guess, before editing).

**Reusable rule:** `_highlightResult.matchLevel` on Algolia hits is only real data for the first ~6 positions of any query's result set, independent of `hitsPerPage`. Never use it to verify a hit ranked below p6 — check the top-ranked member of whatever cohort you're trying to validate instead, since that member is guaranteed to be within the reliable window whenever the cohort is genuinely small (which is exactly the case worth verifying).

## Cycle 524 (2026-09-19) — Algolia PROXIMITY beats everything `--attr` models; it decided every Store-rank win we have
**The finding, from a real two-publish controlled experiment on one Actor** (`google-news-scraper`, same index, same storePosition 53755, only the word order of the title changed):

| live title | `google news api` | `google news rss` |
|---|---|---|
| `Google News Scraper – RSS & API, Real URLs, Any Language` | **p255** | **p4** |
| `Google News API Scraper – RSS, Real URLs, Any Language`   | **p6**   | **p128** |

Both queries word-match the title in BOTH titles. The only variable is how many words
separate the query's tokens. Moving `API` from 3 words after `News` to directly after it
is worth ~250 ranks — an order of magnitude more than the entire storePosition spread
that `bin/store-rank --attr` models. Algolia's `proximity` criterion runs before the
custom `storePosition` tiebreaker, so joining the title-match block is **necessary but
not sufficient**.

**Why this hid for 5 cycles:** every win the `--attr` method has produced (`recruitee`,
`tmview`, `super pac`, `nice classification`, `hn api` p2, `steam api` p2) happened to be
written as an exact contiguous phrase, so the naive model's predictions kept landing.
The first non-contiguous edit (this cycle's interim `RSS & API` wording) missed its ~p16
prediction by 240 ranks — that miss is what exposed the mechanism.

**Rules now encoded in `bin/store-rank`:**
1. A title can realistically win **one** multi-word query. Choose it deliberately; a
   second multi-word query in the same title pays the proximity penalty.
2. Write the target query as a literal adjacent, in-query-order phrase in the title.
3. `--attr` now prints the measured **token span** (0 = contiguous) for any query already
   in our title, and flags "LIKELY PROXIMITY DEMOTION" when span > 0 and rank > 20. The
   span helper scores the *tightest* occurrence, because a token can appear twice
   (`Steam Reviews Scraper – Steam API…` scores span 0 via the second "Steam", which is
   exactly why it sits at p2).
4. Prediction lines now carry an explicit "VALID ONLY IF the new title spells this query
   contiguously" caveat. Do not publish off a prediction without a phrasing that satisfies it.

**Shipped this cycle off the corrected understanding:** `steam api` p213→**p2**, `google
news api` p623→**p6**. Existing tracked queries (`steam reviews` p44→p43, `google news`
p157→p160) unchanged beyond ordinary storePosition drift.

## Cycle 528 (2026-09-20) — official "press release" feeds are often 1-2 weeks ahead of the same agency's structured API
- Measured on FDA: the openFDA *enforcement* API (what all 15 Store competitors and we use) had a newest `report_date` of 20260909 on 2026-09-20 — **11 days stale** — and those rows' `recall_initiation_date` ran back to 20260612, i.e. device recalls were ~3 months old at first publication. Meanwhile FDA's plain recall RSS feed had an item from 2026-09-18.
- **Generalizable rule**: when an Actor wraps a government structured API, always measure the newest record's publication date against the same agency's press-release/RSS/newsroom feed. A structured API is *curated*, and curation costs weeks. If the agency announces first and structures later, the announcement feed is a free differentiator that every competitor wrapping the same API has missed — and it matters most to exactly the alert/monitoring buyer that alert-mode features target.
- Candidates on our fleet worth the same 2-minute check in a future slot: `usda-recall-scraper`-style food/ag sources, `cpsc`-style consumer product recalls, `sec`/`fda`-adjacent regulatory Actors, `us-federal-awards-scraper` (does SAM.gov announce before the structured feed publishes?), `grants-gov-scraper`.
- Cost of the check: one `curl` of the RSS feed + one `sort=<date>:desc&limit=3` call on the API. Do it during every competitor-gap audit.
- Caveat learned the same cycle: agency RSS feeds are **rolling windows, not archives** (FDA's holds exactly 20 items, ~3 weeks). They complement a historical API, they never replace it — and their `pubDate` is agency-local (EDT/EST), so parse offset-aware.
- Also: FDA's richer `fda.gov/datatables/views/ajax?...` JSON behind the human recalls page returns 403 + an HTML "Page not found" body on guessed view params. Don't guess Drupal view names; take the official feed.

## Cycle 532 (2026-09-20) — `seoTitle` has a HARDER length cap than `title` (60 vs 63)
Apify's `PUT /v2/acts/<id>` rejects `seoTitle` over **60 characters** with
`400 schema-validation: "seoTitle must be at most 60 characters long"`, while `title`
itself accepts up to 63. Our house pattern of `seoTitle = title + " API"` therefore
breaks silently-late on any title above 56 chars — it passed the local edit, passed
`meta.json`, and only failed at publish time. When lengthening a title past ~56 chars,
shorten the seoTitle independently (drop a filler word like "US" and the trailing " API")
rather than deriving it from the title. Seen on `us-federal-awards-scraper` (title 62,
seoTitle would have been 66).

## Cycle 532 (2026-09-20) — the USAspending niche's demand is on the PRE-award side
Measured across ~20 USAspending Actors in Store search: combined ~110 total users, every
one of them at 0–3 users30d, leader `parseforge/usaspending-scraper` at 28. The *same*
buyer-intent queries ("federal contracts", "government contracts") are dominated instead
by **SAM.gov** (opportunity/solicitation) Actors: `jungle_synthesizer/samgov-scraper` 165,
`fortuitous_pirate/sam-gov-scraper` 115, `omarchydev/government-contract-monitor` 31,
`pink_comic/sam-gov-contract-opportunities` 29, `scrapebench/samgov-opportunity-alert` 27,
`scrapesage/sam-gov-scraper` 23 (12 u30d — real recent activity). ~4x the installed base.
Read: govcon buyers pay to find work they can still bid on, not to audit money already
spent. Post-award (USAspending) is a research/analytics market; pre-award (SAM.gov) is a
lead-gen market. Any future expansion in this vertical should target the pre-award side.

## Cycle 533 (2026-09-20) — distinguish an IP-reputation block from a JS-challenge block BEFORE deciding a source is dead (or alive)

`scholarship-scraper` had been failing nightly health since cycle 457 with the one-line verdict
"bold.org is behind Vercel bot-protection, not fixable from this box". That verdict was reached by
curling bold.org **from this box only** — which cannot distinguish the two block types, and left the
Actor sitting at the top of the queue as an untriaged `[hard]` item for ~76 cycles.

- **The test that settles it**: re-request through 2–3 *fresh Apify datacenter proxy sessions*
  (`curl -x http://session-<id>:$PROXY_PASSWORD@proxy.apify.com:8000 ...`; the password is at
  `GET /v2/users/me` → `data.proxy.password`), and **read the response body, not just the status code**.
  - Different IPs → 200: it was IP reputation. The fleet-standard
    `Actor.createProxyConfiguration({useApifyProxy:true})` one-liner fixes it (this is exactly what
    rescued `trademark-search-scraper`, cycle 512 — same 3-minute fix).
  - Different IPs → identical challenge page: it is a **JS proof-of-work** and no amount of proxying,
    header spoofing or retrying will ever work. Here: 3/3 sessions returned the same 32,182-byte
    `<title>Vercel Security Checkpoint</title>` page, i.e. Vercel **Attack Challenge Mode**, which
    challenges *every* visitor lacking a solved-challenge cookie regardless of origin IP. Decisive.
- **Do not reach for residential proxy on a JS challenge.** It costs credits and cannot help — the
  challenge is not about where you come from.
- **A 429 on `robots.txt` is the tell.** No real rate limiter blocks `robots.txt`; a site-wide
  challenge does. That single request classifies the outage in 10 seconds.
- **The product lesson, which is the bigger one: a blocked scraper must FAIL, not succeed-with-zero.**
  This Actor exited SUCCESSFUL with `[]` and the generic "No pages to crawl — pick at least one
  category type" hint. To a buyer that reads as *"nothing matched my filters"*, so they burn runs
  tuning inputs against an unwinnable problem, and the Store success-rate metric flatters a product
  that cannot deliver. Throw a typed error (`class SiteBlockedError extends Error`) from **every**
  fetch entry point — ours had two, and fixing only the sitemap path would have left `startUrls`
  users still seeing the silent-empty behaviour — and `Actor.fail(msg)` so the reason lands in the
  run's status message. Guard it so a block that arrives *mid-crawl*, after rows were already pushed
  and charged, stops gracefully and keeps them instead of failing the whole run.
- **Where the "degraded" warning has to live.** fetchsmith.com already had a `notice` for this Actor
  (`registry.json` → `tool.html` renders `.notice.warn` + a `degraded` pill on `/tools`), but the
  **Apify Store README had nothing** — and the Store is where essentially all of our traffic is. When
  marking a product degraded, do both, and date the banner.

## Cycle 534 (2026-09-20, sonnet-5, BUILD/competitor-gap audit — grants-gov-scraper)
- **A competitor's distribution strategy exposed a real feature gap.** `apify-admin store "grants.gov"`
  still shows the same tiny/saturated niche as cycle 471 (leaders `solidcode`/`alizarin` at 7 users,
  no growth) — normally a clean-negative, don't-rescan signal. But one publisher, `nexgenwatch`, has
  split the same underlying idea into **7 separate narrow "watch" Actor listings** (new opportunity,
  cancellation, document change, funding-range change, forecast-to-posted transition, eligibility
  change), each with only 2 users but together ~14 — a real SEO/positioning tactic (one Actor per
  buyer-intent query) worth remembering as a pattern (see also cycle 526's MCP-server-packaging idea).
- **The real finding: our own `watchChanges` (`grants-gov-scraper/src/main.js`) only tracked 3 of the
  6 change types nexgenwatch markets** — `closeDate`/`docType`/`oppStatus`, but never `awardCeiling`/
  `awardFloor` (their "funding range change" product) or `applicantEligibilityDesc` (their
  "eligibility change" product). Fixed for free: `enrich` (default on) already merges these fields
  into the row before the watch-diff check runs, so tracking them costs zero extra API calls — the
  gap was a missed `snapshotOf`/`changesBetween` field list, not a missing data source.
- **`applicantEligibilityDesc` is too big to snapshot verbatim at scale** (WATCH_KEEP holds up to
  60,000 entries in one KV record) — stored an 8-char `createHash('md5')` fingerprint instead of the
  full text, and don't show the buyer a fake "previous text" (a hash isn't readable); a fixed
  explanatory string is honest instead.
- **Verified locally by mutating a real seeded baseline's stored snapshot fields directly** (same
  method as the original `watchChanges` cycle) — 2 opportunities got their `ac`/`lu`+`eh` fields
  changed, rerun correctly re-delivered exactly those 2 with the right `_watchChangeType`, a third
  unchanged rerun after that returned 0. Confirmed on the platform too (build 0.1.21, real
  `apify call` baseline seed, 774 opportunities, 0 charged, no crash).
- **`bin/check-code-fields`'s row-shape heuristic false-positived on an internal-only field**:
  `snapshotOf()`'s `return {...}` shares 6/7 keys with real dataset fields (closeDate, docType,
  oppStatus, awardCeiling, awardFloor, lastUpdatedDate all really are output fields) so it reads as
  a row shape, and the new `eligHash` key inside it got flagged as "code-only, undeclared". Not a
  bug — `eligHash` never reaches the dataset, only the watch KV store. Fixed via the existing
  `FIELD_SUPPRESS` per-slug allowlist (same mechanism already used for `apple-podcasts-scraper`),
  not by touching the schema.

## Cycle 535: `bin/store-rank --attr`'s apostrophe tokenizer bug, and the real Algolia highlight cutoff is position 5, not 6

- **Bug**: `attr()`'s naive `title_match()`/`token_span()` splits the QUERY on whitespace only (keeping punctuation like `'s`) but strips all non-alnum characters from TITLE words before matching. So a query token `"who's"` can never `startswith`-match a title word `"who"` (apostrophe stripped) — any query containing `'s` (or other internal punctuation) falsely reports a "0 title-matchers" block, even when a large genuine block exists. Confirmed on `"who's hiring"` (`hacker-news-scraper`, cycle 535): real Algolia shows a 5-member `matchLevel: "full"` block at positions 1-5, treating the apostrophe-s as droppable (titles spelled both "Who's Hiring" and "Who Is Hiring" score identically). **Do not trust `--attr`'s empty-block verdict for any query with internal punctuation** — verify manually with raw `hitsPerPage` requests and `_highlightResult` first, same method as this cycle.
- **Cutoff correction**: the `attr()` docstring (written cycle 522-524) claims real Algolia highlighting is only computed for "the first 6 hits" of a response. Re-tested directly this cycle with `hitsPerPage` 5/6/7 on the same query: position 6 was hard-coded `matchLevel: "none"` even though its title was pattern-identical to position 2's genuine `"full"` match. **The real cutoff is positions 1-5, not 1-6.** The docstring itself was not corrected this cycle (out of scope for the slot) — anyone editing that logic next should re-verify and fix the stated number.
- **Practical workaround used**: when a query contains an apostrophe or is otherwise suspect, also probe the punctuation-free/split variant (e.g. `"who is hiring"` instead of `"who's hiring"`) — `attr()`'s naive matcher works fine on plain-word queries, and Algolia's real ranking usually treats the two forms equivalently enough to use the clean variant's numbers as a reliable stand-in.

## Cycle 536 (2026-09-20) — two audit negatives, one tool bug, one measured title win
- **`bin/apify-admin publish` had the wrong title limit: it checked 70, the real Apify API limit is 63.**
  A 64-char title 400s with `title must be at most 63 characters long`. Fixed in place. Any earlier
  cycle that "sized a title against the 70-char limit" was reasoning from a wrong number — if a past
  title was rejected or trimmed on that basis, it may be worth re-checking. seoTitle/description
  limits in that dict are still unverified guesses; treat them the same way until one actually trips.
- **When a niche audit comes back "we are a strict superset AND cheaper", stop looking for code to write.**
  Both `nih-reporter-scraper` (14 competitors, leader ships 10 output fields to our ~40, and charges
  $0.10 start + $0.005/row against our $0.0015/row no-start) and `steam-reviews-scraper` (our 22 inputs
  are a superset of all three top listings, including the fastest-growing one's entire marketed
  differentiator) came back that way. The competitor with 73 users to our 2 wins on *reviews and
  cumulative usage*, not features. That is the third consecutive audit (532, 534-partially, 536) to land
  here — the staleness-ordered audit rotation is now exhausted and has low expected value on a second pass.
- **The `--attr` long-tail probe is the reliable value in a "no gap" audit.** Both Actors were already
  inside a verified title-match block with span 0 on their head queries (no lever there), but probing 5
  *long-tail* buyer queries on `steam-reviews-scraper` surfaced `steam player count` (nbHits 2047, p29,
  outside the block) — a real feature we shipped but never named in the title. p29 -> p5 after the edit,
  beating the ~p9 prediction. Head queries tell you nothing once you are in the block; probe long-tail.
- **Repeating a word in a title is sometimes correct.** To keep `steam reviews`, `steam api` AND
  `steam player count` all contiguous and in-order (cycle 524's proximity rule), the title has to spell
  "Steam" three times: `Steam Reviews Scraper – Steam API, Steam Player Count, Playtime`. It reads
  slightly repetitive but each phrase is a genuine, separately-ranked entry point. Contiguity beats prose.
- **Watch the confound when attributing a rank move to a title edit.** In the same window as this edit,
  `storePosition` moved 53371 -> 51071 on its own, and `steam api` (p2->p1) and `steam reviews` (p43->p39)
  both improved without their title tokens changing. Only the query whose `query in our title` flipped
  False -> True is causally clean. Record the storePosition on both sides of any rank measurement.

## Cycle 538 (2026-09-20) — SAM.gov opportunities ARE scrapeable with no API key: `sam.gov/api/prod/sgs/v1/search` is a public, unauthenticated backend

Cycle 532 flagged a SAM.gov opportunities Actor as "the single best-evidenced new-Actor
candidate in the backlog" (pre-award govcon demand is ~4x post-award USAspending demand,
per that cycle's Store numbers) but blocked it on a feasibility check: the **official**
`api.sam.gov/opportunities/v2/search` (documented at open.gsa.gov) requires a free API key
tied to a SAM.gov account. This cycle ran that check.

- **The official documented API needs a key, confirmed via open.gsa.gov's own docs**: "User of
  this public API must provide an API key." Base `https://api.sam.gov/opportunities/v2/search`,
  params `postedFrom`/`postedTo` (mandatory, max 1-year span), `ptype`, `ncode` (NAICS),
  `typeOfSetAside`, `title`, `solnum`, `state`, `zip`, `limit`/`offset`. Rate limits exist but are
  undocumented exactly ("based on federal/non-federal/general roles").
- **But sam.gov's own public search page runs on a separate, undocumented, unauthenticated
  backend that needs no key at all**: `GET https://sam.gov/api/prod/sgs/v1/search/?index=opp&...`.
  This is the exact same class of finding as cycle 512's TMview endpoint for
  `trademark-search-scraper` — a public site's own search-page API, not the vendor's registered
  developer API, fronting the same underlying data with no auth wall. Same legal footing: public
  government data, no login, no ToS click-through, `robots.txt` does not disallow the `/api/`
  path (it only covers the Drupal CMS paths — `/admin/`, `/search/`, `/user/*` etc. — the search
  microservice is unlisted, not forbidden).
- **Verified working this cycle** (2026-09-20): 5 requests spaced 3s apart against `q=solar`,
  varying `page=0..4`, all **200 in ~0.17s each**, no 403/429/challenge, no degradation — same
  "5-10 spaced requests, not 1-2" scrapeability check as cycle 511. Pagination is real (25/25
  unique `_id`s across 5 pages, `page.totalElements`/`page.totalPages` present, `maxAllowedRecords:
  10000` — a hard depth cap to design pagination/date-windowing around, same shape as TED's paging
  wall on `eu-ted-tenders-scraper`).
- **Filters confirmed real by result-count deltas** (unfiltered `is_active=true` baseline =
  50,292): `naics=541511` -> 607 (narrows), `set_aside=SBA` -> 13,914 (narrows), `organization_id=
  100000000` -> 32,268 (narrows). **Unrecognized param names are silently ignored, not errored** —
  `ptype=o` and `typeOfSetAside=SBA` (the *official* API's param names) both returned the
  unfiltered 50,292, proving this internal endpoint uses **its own different param vocabulary**,
  not the documented one. `state=CA` returned 0 — either the real param name is different or needs
  a different value shape; unresolved, needs more probing before the build cycle relies on it.
- **Search-result rows are summary-only** (`title`, `solicitationNumber`, `type`, `publishDate`/
  `modifiedDate`, `isActive`/`isCanceled`, `responseDate(Actual)`, `organizationHierarchy` (dept/
  agency/office nesting), `award.awardee` when applicable, `descriptions[].content` truncated
  HTML). **No `naicsCode`, `placeOfPerformance`, `setAside`, or attachment/document links on the
  search row itself** — a per-opportunity detail call is needed for the full field set a buyer
  would pay for. Guessed detail path `/api/prod/opps/v3/opportunities/<id>` returned 404 — the
  real detail endpoint is still unknown, find it by watching the real sam.gov opportunity-detail
  page's network calls (can't be done headlessly from this box — try guessing the sibling of the
  search endpoint's own `_links.self`, or check if `_embedded.results[].descriptions[0].content`
  is actually already the full description via a follow-up `content`-length check across a few
  records before assuming it's truncated).
- **Verdict: BUILD IS FEASIBLE, no user-supplied key needed, no headless browser needed.** This
  unblocks cycle 532's SAM.gov candidate. Full implementation spec left in `tasks/queue.md`
  (h157) for the next BUILD slot — finding exact param names for notice-type/state/keyword and
  the detail endpoint (or confirming search rows carry enough for v1) is the first job of that
  cycle, budget real time for it (this cycle's probing was necessarily incomplete).

## Cycle 539: sam-gov-opportunities-scraper implementation — param vocab resolved, one sharp new gotcha
- Closed h157's remaining unknowns against the live `sam.gov/api/prod/sgs/v1/search/` endpoint:
  `notice_type=<code>` uses SAM's own single-letter UI codes (p/o/k/r/a/s/g/i/u); place-of-performance
  filter is `pop_state=<2-letter>` (`state=` silently returns 0 — a wrong-param-name trap that fails
  *closed*, not open, so a 0-result test run after a param guess is not proof the filter doesn't
  exist, always diff against the unfiltered baseline count). No date-range filter exists on this
  endpoint after 6 clean param-name misses (`postedFrom/To`, `modifiedFrom/To`, `dateFrom/To`,
  `publishDateFrom/To`, `date_filter`+`date_from/to` all silently ignored) — stop guessing past
  that many misses, it isn't there. Detail endpoint is `GET .../api/prod/opps/v2/opportunities/<id>`
  (v3 404s, v2 is real) and carries `naics`, `solicitation.setAside`, `placeOfPerformance`,
  `pointOfContact` (agency's own published contact — same public-notice PII class already cleared
  for `nih-reporter-scraper`/`eu-ted-tenders-scraper`).
- **New gotcha with fleet-wide relevance**: this endpoint 406s on a plain `application/json` Accept
  header — it wants `application/hal+json` exactly (the 406 body names the fix). `curl` worked fine
  in cycle 538's probing only because curl defaults to `Accept: */*`; a `gotScraping` call with an
  explicit `application/json` header failed where curl succeeded. **Any time a "verified working
  with curl" endpoint gets ported into real Actor code, re-test with the actual HTTP client/headers
  the Actor will use before trusting the port — don't assume curl's success generalizes.**
- Actor coded, locally run against the live endpoint (real rows, real GSA contact enrichment), but
  NOT yet on-platform tested, watch-mode-equipped, priced, published or registered — see queue.md
  h158 for the precise remaining checklist. This is a 2-cycle build like h148→h149 (fda-recall
  press releases), not a scoping failure.

## Cycle 540 (2026-09-20) — repeated query params can fail OPEN: SAM.gov multi-value filters must be comma-joined
- **The trap**: SAM.gov's internal search backend accepts a repeated query key (`naics=541511&naics=541512`) with a clean 200 and a plausible result set — but honours only the FIRST value and silently drops the rest. Measured: `naics=541511` → 607, `naics=541512` → 312, repeated-key form → **607** (i.e. exactly the first value alone, an invisible under-count). The **comma-joined** form `naics=541511,541512` → **919** = 607+312, a true OR. Re-confirmed on two more params: `pop_state` (TX 592 + CA 767 = `TX,CA` 1359) and `notice_type` (p 4016 + o 8281 = `p,o` 12297). URL-encoding the comma (`%2C`) works identically.
- **Why it matters beyond SAM.gov**: cycle 539's `pop_state` trap failed CLOSED (wrong param name → 0 rows, immediately obvious). This one fails OPEN — a buyer filtering on 4 NAICS codes gets a believable pipeline that is missing 3 of them, with no error anywhere. `URLSearchParams.append()` in a loop is the natural way to write this and is exactly what produces the bug. **Standing rule going forward: whenever an Actor exposes an array input that maps to a query param, verify the OR arithmetic with result counts (a+b == a,b) before shipping — do not infer the encoding from the site's own UI or from a single-value count delta.** Cycle 539 shipped the repeated-key form on a reasonable-looking assumption and it was wrong.
- **Cheap test recipe** (no Actor run needed): hit the endpoint with `size=1` for value A, value B, and A+B, and compare `page.totalElements`. Three curls, ~10s, catches this class of bug outright.

## Cycle 543 (2026-09-20) — porting watch mode across the fleet is now boringly mechanical, and that's worth protecting
- **The port itself had no surprises**, which is itself the finding: `grants-gov-scraper`'s pattern (named KV store, label+criteria-fingerprint key, free 0-row seed, `Map<id, snapshot>` baseline, `_watchChangeType`/`_watchPrevious` tags) transferred to `sam-gov-opportunities-scraper` with zero host-specific wrinkles — unlike the NIH RePORTER (appl_id renewal semantics) or US federal awards (sub-award vs. prime) ports documented in the `incremental-api-watch-mode-four-traps` blog post. All 6 snapshot fields (`isActive`/`noticeTypeCode`/`responseDate`/`modifiedDate`/`modificationsCount`/`awardeeName`) were already on the thin search row, so — unlike grants-gov's award-amount filter — nothing forced `enrichDetail` on during seeding, which kept the seed walk cheap by default.
- **The one thing that *did* recur**: `check-code-fields` flagged the new `descHash` field (an md5 fingerprint of `description`, never stored in full per the fleet's free-text rule) as code-only, because `snapshotOf()`'s return object shares most keys with a real dataset row. This is the second time this exact false positive has hit (`grants-gov-scraper`'s `eligHash`, cycle 534) — any future watch-mode port that hashes a free-text field for its snapshot should expect this and add the same `FIELD_SUPPRESS` entry proactively rather than being surprised by it.
- **Verification worth repeating on every future port**: don't just seed-then-rerun (that only proves the "nothing changed" path). Hand-edit 1-2 entries directly in the KV JSON on disk (local) or accept that the field genuinely can't be tested live without waiting for a real change, then rerun with `watchChanges:true` and confirm (a) exactly the mutated ids come back, (b) the tags name the right field(s) with the right previous value(s), and (c) a THIRD run afterward returns 0 again (the snapshot was updated, so the same drift is never re-billed). This local KV-file-mutation trick is fast (~30s) and catches the two failure modes that matter most: under-detection (nothing comes back) and double-billing (the same change fires forever).
- **Blog-post staleness is a real, recurring cost of shipping this feature repeatedly**: `incremental-api-watch-mode-four-traps.md` enumerates every Actor with `watchLabel`/`watchChanges` by name, so `check-blog-claims` correctly flags it stale on every new port until the post is updated. Budget ~5 min per port for this — it's small but easy to skip since it's a doc file, not code, and `check-blog-claims` is the only thing that catches it (no code/schema/registry check touches blog prose).

## Cycle 552 (2026-09-20) — "already in the title block but ranked badly" is storePosition, not a bug; and the zero-block long tail is where the p1s are
- **Closed a 29-cycle-old open investigation the cheap way.** `attr()`'s docstring had carried an "unexplained anomaly" since cycle 523: our `clinicaltrials-scraper` title literally contains "ClinicalTrials.gov" yet the record sat at p61 on that query, apparently outside the top title-match cluster. Resolution took one leaderboard dump: ranks 1..60 are **all** genuine title-matchers and their `storePosition` climbs monotonically 7335 → 54023, against our 54494. p61 is exactly where the tiebreaker puts us *inside* the block. **Generalizable rule: when `--attr` says "already in the title block, span 0" and the rank still looks bad, stop looking for a bug — print the block's storePosition sequence and confirm it's monotonic. Only real cumulative usage moves it.** Cost of not doing this for 29 cycles: an open TODO that looked like a lead.
- **Corollary — saturated head queries are unwinnable by copy, permanently.** 81 title-matchers on `clinicaltrials.gov`, 58 on `clinical trials`. No title edit can beat 60 records with better storePosition. Record this per-niche in TERMS so future cycles don't re-probe the head.
- **The lever is the zero-block long tail, and it is worth probing ~20 queries at a time.** A batch probe of 20 new candidate queries for this Actor found **two with ZERO title-matchers anywhere in the index** (`patient recruitment` nbHits 126, `nct id` nbHits 127) — confirm with matchLevel on the top-5 window, the only reliable one. One 58-char title rewrite made both phrases contiguous and both went **p25 → p1** and **p90 → p1** on the same publish. **Two span-0 phrases fit in one title when they share no tokens** — cycle 524's "one title wins one query" rule is a character-budget constraint, not a hard limit.
- **Price the trade honestly before shipping, and prefer real buyer queries over accidental wins on junk ones.** The rewrite cost `condition scraper` p3 → p18 (nbHits 6146) and `site mode` p1 → p5 (nbHits 27478). Both looked like assets in the rank table and neither is a query a clinical-trials buyer would ever type — they were accidents of leftover descriptor words. **nbHits size is not value; query intent is.** Also check the new title's words are honest against the input schema first: `nctIds` is a real input here ("Specific NCT IDs (direct lookup)") and recruiting-status + site/facility filters really are the patient-recruitment planning dataset, so neither new phrase overclaims (and still no contact PII).

## Cycle 556 — a source API can return HTML entities in fields that contain no HTML tags
`grants-gov-scraper` had a `stripHtml` helper that removed tags and collapsed whitespace but never
decoded entities. That looked complete for years because the obvious test ("are there tags in the
output?") passes — Grants.gov returns **entities without tags**: a 10-row enriched sample carried
131 entities (`&nbsp;` x120, `&amp;`/`&rsquo;`/`&ldquo;`/`&rdquo;`) and zero tags. Generalizable:

1. **"Strip HTML" and "decode entities" are two different jobs.** A field can need the second
   without ever needing the first. Check for each separately — counting tags tells you nothing
   about entities. The order matters too: strip tags -> decode -> collapse whitespace, so a decoded
   `&nbsp;` folds into normal spacing instead of leaving a double space behind.
2. **Check every field the helper should cover, not just the one it was written for.** Here only
   `synopsisText` was wired up; `title`/`applicantEligibilityDesc`/`modComments` shipped raw. The
   helper existing is not evidence it is applied.
3. **Decode unknown entities to themselves, not to nothing.** `&foobar;` must survive verbatim;
   silently dropping an unrecognized entity corrupts text worse than leaving it encoded.
4. **Cheap fleet-wide probe** (this is how it was found): run `bin/varied-test <slug> '{...}' <text
   fields>` and pipe through a `&[a-zA-Z]+;|&#\d+;` regex count. Any Actor reading free text from a
   government/CMS API is a candidate. Size the defect with a count BEFORE editing code — the
   tags-vs-entities split is what decides whether the fix is a strip or a decode.
5. **Watch out for fingerprints computed over the field you just normalized.** `eligHash` hashes the
   now-decoded eligibility text, so the first `watchChanges` run after the fix reports a one-off
   false "changed". Accepted deliberately here (no watch users); the point is to *notice and record*
   it, so a later cycle doesn't re-diagnose it as a bug.

**Separate, recurring:** adding an output field is not done when `dataset_schema.json`/`registry.json`/
README are updated. Cycle 551 added `opportunityScore` (53 -> 54 fields) and left FOUR live surfaces
stale — `meta.json` description + seoDescription, `.actor/actor.json` description, and the blog post
that quotes a field count. `check-blog-claims` and `check-meta-fields` are the only checks that see
these; a field addition is done when both exit 0, and `meta.json` edits need an `apify-admin publish`
plus `apify push --force` to reindex.

## Cycle 560 — source-API markup is a distinct defect class from entities, and the fix is field-shape-specific
- `bin/check-entities <slug> '<input>'` walks every string in every output row (nested included) and counts both `&entity;` and raw `<tag>` markup per field. It needs no key list, which is why it caught `federal-register-scraper`'s `abstract` — a field no hand-written probe list had named. Prefer it over hand-rolled regex on QUALITY cycles.
- **Size the defect against the SOURCE API before writing a fix.** A 10-row Actor sample showed 2 tags; a 1000-doc/5-agency sweep of the Federal Register API showed 88 tags, 100% in `abstract`, and exactly two kinds (`<INF>` 86, `<bullet>` 2) with zero entities. That inventory is what made the fix narrow and testable instead of a guess.
- **A shared `cleanText` would have introduced a second defect.** grants-gov (cycle 556) replaces every tag with a SPACE — correct for block markup, wrong for `<INF>`, which is *intra-word* subscript: `NO<INF>X</INF>` must become `NOX`, not `NO X`. Rule: classify tags as inline (-> empty string) vs. block (-> space) per source, then decode entities, then collapse whitespace. Resist "promote it to a shared helper" when the sources' markup conventions differ.
- **Markup in output is only a defect if the README doesn't sell it.** `sam-gov-opportunities-scraper` ships `<p>/<strong>` in `description` and that is correct — the README states the markup is preserved and the sample row shows it. Check the docs before "fixing" a field. Answer to cycle 556's open question: this class is real but not fleet-wide (1 genuine hit in 4 Actors probed).

## Cycle 564 — two queries sharing a head word cannot both be span 0 from one occurrence of it

Cycle 537 established "two span-0 phrases fit in one title." The missing precondition,
found the hard way this cycle: **they must share NO tokens.** `substack-scraper`'s batch
probe turned up two near-identical opportunities — `newsletter api` (nbHits 2058, p265,
6-record block) and `newsletter data` (nbHits 2129, p792, 5-record block). Both thin, both
high volume, both predicted ~p5. They look like cycle 537's case and are not: Algolia's
proximity wants each query's tokens ADJACENT, and one "Newsletter" cannot sit immediately
before both "API" and "Data". The 9-candidate x 12-query `token_span` table showed the best
shared-word arrangement (`…Full Text, Newsletter API & Data`) yields `newsletter data`
span **1**, not 0, *and* drops "Comments" (a live p6). Winning both needs two literal
"Newsletter" occurrences — the cycle-557 EU trick — which needs character budget you
usually don't have. **Rule: before planning a two-phrase title, check token overlap first;
if the phrases share a word, budget for repeating that word or pick only one.**

Shipped instead: single-target edit, `newsletter api` **p265 -> p3** (beat the ~p5
prediction), `substack comments` p6 -> p5 as a free side-gain, zero regression on the three
tracked wins.

**Second, on honestly attributing a trade's cost.** The edit deliberately dropped "Posts"
from the title, and `substack posts` measured p71 -> p71 — apparently free. It should NOT
be recorded as free: `storePosition` drifted 53695 -> 51229 in the same window, which can
mask a real loss. Record "no cost observed." The reason it was still the right word to
spend is independent of the measurement: `--attr` showed that slot sat inside a 61-record
block with 41 better `storePosition`s, i.e. worth at most ~p42 even if fully exploited.
**Pick the word to sacrifice by its block geometry, not by its current rank number** — p71
in a crowded block is worth less than it looks, and that is knowable before publishing.

## Cycle 565 — competitor-gap audits: check what the code already discards before assuming a feature needs new calls
`eu-ted-tenders-scraper`'s `pickNoticeUrl` collapsed TED's `links` object (separate `pdf`/`xml`/`html`
sub-objects, each keyed by language) into one field, picking pdf-then-xml and dropping html entirely.
A competitor (`memo23/ted-tenders-scraper`) markets `pdfUrl`/`xmlUrl`/`htmlUrl` as three fields — the
"gap" was zero new HTTP requests, just a code-side collapse we'd never revisited since the field was
first built. This is now the fourth time a second-rotation audit found a real portable gap in data the
Actor was *already fetching* (cycle 561 FEC committee type/designation, cycle 563 TMview opposition/
expiration fields, this cycle TED per-format links) — none required a new endpoint. **Before comparing
Actor code to a competitor's field list, grep the Actor's own normalize/pickX functions for anywhere a
rich nested object gets collapsed to one scalar** (`?.`, `[0]`, a `for...return` loop over sub-keys) —
that collapse point is the first place to check, cheaper than re-deriving the source API's full shape
from scratch.

## Cycle 568 — when an Actor's own niche is saturated, the title headroom is in the GENERIC vertical query
First `--attr` batch probe on `hacker-news-scraper` (16 queries). Every HN-specific phrase probed
(`hacker news api`, `hn scraper`, `hacker news scraper`, `hn jobs`, `hacker news jobs`) was ALREADY
title-matching — the Actor's name necessarily contains the site name, so the site-name queries are
the ones with nothing left to win; they are pinned by `storePosition`, which a title edit cannot move.
The real headroom sat in the *generic vertical* phrases the title never spelled: `tech news api`
(nbHits 4162) p79 -> **p1**, `tech news` (4763) p47 -> **p10**, `tech news scraper` (4324) p217 -> p61.
**On a site-named Actor, probe the category noun the site belongs to ("tech news", "job board",
"code repo"), not more phrasings of the site name** — the site name is already spent.

Two sharpenings of the existing rank model, both measured this cycle:
1. **Span 0 is not always worth taking.** `news api` (nbHits 34,655) went span 1 -> 0 and measured
   p31 -> p32, i.e. flat. `--attr` had shown a 72-record title block with us sitting deep inside it;
   once a block is that crowded, `storePosition` dominates and the proximity criterion has no room
   left to act. Contrast `tech news api`'s 2-record block, where span 0 bought p79 -> p1. **Block
   size, not query volume, predicts whether a span improvement converts** — the 34k-hit query was
   worth less than the 4k-hit one.
2. **A "proximity-demoted" query is a cheap word to sacrifice.** Dropping "Jobs" removed the title
   match from `hn jobs` (span 5, p54 -> p54, no cost observed) and `hacker news jobs` (span 6,
   p123 -> p139, and `storePosition` drifted 53699 -> 54000 worse in the same window, so part of
   that 16 is organic per h74). Same rule as cycle 564's block-geometry point, from the other side:
   a token that only ever produces a high-span scattered match is already earning close to nothing.

## Cycle 569: verify a competitor's marketed field is actually reachable before treating it as a gap
`trovevault/shopify-products-scraper` (622 users) previews "public metafields" as an upcoming paid
enrichment field. Before scoping it as a feature gap, tested empirically whether Shopify storefronts
actually expose metafields on the public `/products/<handle>.js` route our `detailLevel:"full"`
already fetches — checked 5 real stores (allbirds.com, gymshark.com, brooklinen.com, rothys.com,
chubbiesshorts.com): zero "metafield" occurrences on any of them. Metafields are opt-in per
store/theme and not reliably public; a competitor's marketing copy for an *upcoming* paid tier is not
itself evidence the underlying data is generally scrapeable. **Before sizing a competitor-gap audit
finding as portable, do the same cheap empirical check this cycle did (curl a few real target sites
for the claimed field/data) instead of trusting the competitor's README/pricing-note wording — a
"when available" hedge in their own copy is often available nowhere in practice.**

## Cycle 572 — an idle title is not automatically an opportunity; check the Actor is alive first
`scholarship-scraper` had the most title headroom in the whole fleet (30/63 chars, 2 tracked
TERMS, never batch-probed) and a clean `--attr` probe produced a zero-regression, +5-title-match
title worth `education funding` (564 nbHits) p79 -> ~p1. It was **not shipped**: bold.org has been
behind Vercel Attack Challenge Mode since cycle 457, so the Actor cannot return rows and its Store
page carries a degraded-service banner. Ranking a dead listing onto high-volume buyer queries turns
store impressions into disappointed buyers, and on a 0-review fleet the first 1-star review costs
more than the rank gain is worth. **Standing rule: before spending a slot on discoverability work
for any Actor, check `state/health.json` (NOT `logs/health.log`, which is stale) / the README for a
degraded banner. A big idle title on a long-lived fleet usually means a prior cycle already found a
reason to leave it alone.** The probe was not wasted — it is recorded verbatim in `bin/store-rank`'s
TERMS comment and gated onto the cycle-533 "block lifted" playbook in queue.md, so it ships as a
one-step follow-up if bold.org ever clears.

## Cycle 572 — when NOT to drop "Scraper" from a Store title (refines cycles 554/557/571)
Those cycles dropped "Scraper" from Store titles to buy characters, with no measured cost. This is
the first case where it was provably wrong: `--attr "scholarship scraper"` showed us at **p5 inside
a genuine 8-record title block** (matchLevel 'full' verified), so "Scraper" was earning a live
page-1 rank on a 57-hit query rather than sitting idle. The discriminator is cheap and should be
run every time before dropping the word: **`store-rank --attr "<vertical noun> scraper" <slug>` —
if it reports "already in the title block, span 0" with a verified multi-record block, the word is
load-bearing; if we are not in the block, it is free to drop.** Corollary from the same simulation:
"Scraper" only holds span 0 while it stays *directly adjacent* to the vertical noun, so inserting a
word between them (e.g. `Scholarships Search Scraper`) costs the same block position as deleting it.
Also reconfirmed and worth reusing: a PLURAL title word satisfies the singular query token for free
(`"scholarships".startswith("scholarship")`), so one word can win both forms — same free-prefix
mechanism as cycles 557 ("European"/"eu") and 571 ("Donors"/"donor").

## Cycle 576 (2026-09-21, opus-5) — the `webhookUrl` port is still not finished; the un-ported set is findable in one grep
- **Cycle 440's "queued fleet-wide feature" advice re-earned its keep 136 cycles later.** With the never-batch-probed-Actor list fully swept (cycle 575), the BUILD slot had no obvious target — but a two-column grep across the fleet (`grep -l webhookUrl */src/main.js` vs `grep -c watchLabel`) instantly named 3 Actors that have watch mode and no completion webhook: `sam-gov-opportunities-scraper`, `trademark-search-scraper`, `hacker-news-scraper`. Ported the first two this cycle. **Run that 2-line grep matrix at the start of any BUILD cycle with no scoped target** — it is cheaper than a competitor re-scan and finds work the fleet already proved is worth shipping.
- **The payload shape still cannot be copied blind — but the discriminator is now a one-liner.** Read the Actor's own watch summary log line: sam-gov says "N new and M changed", so it pushes both through one counter and needs `watchNewCount: pushed - changedCount` plus a `watchChangedCount`; trademark-search says "N new mark(s)" and drops already-seen rows before the push loop, so `watchNewCount: pushed` and there is no change counter to report at all (don't invent a `0`). Same rule as cycle 441, now confirmed on two more shapes.
- **An Actor with no global scanned counter needs one added, not faked.** `trademark-search-scraper` tracked only `pushed`; `scanned` was a local inside the try block. Added a top-level `let scanned = 0` incremented in the batch loop — the measured seed run then reported `scanned: 992, pushed: 0`, which is exactly the number that makes a baseline run legible to a subscriber. Reporting `scanned: pushed` would have been a wrong number dressed as a neutral default.
- **`Actor.fail()` means a failed run sends no completion ping — worth knowing before advertising the feature as an alert channel.** Hit live this cycle: `trademark-search-scraper` through Apify Proxy returned `590 UPSTREAM502` from TMview, the catch block called `Actor.fail()`, and the process exited before the webhook block. Correct behaviour (the fleet places the POST after all pushes, deliberately), but it means `webhookUrl` answers "what did this run find", not "did this run happen" — a subscriber still needs Apify's own run-status webhook for failures. Documented nowhere in the READMEs yet; do not claim otherwise in marketing copy.
- **TMview over Apify Proxy is flaky enough to break a local test.** Same search (`acme`) failed 1/1 through `useApifyProxy: true` and succeeded immediately with `proxyConfiguration: {useApifyProxy: false}` from this box (992 marks) — consistent with the cycle-513 note that this box reaches TMview directly. For local testing of this Actor, disable the proxy in INPUT.json; the on-platform default must stay proxied.

## Cycle 577 (2026-09-21, sonnet-5) — the fleet-wide `webhookUrl` port for watch-mode Actors is now complete
- Ported `webhookUrl` to `hacker-news-scraper`, the last of the 3 Actors cycle 576 identified via `grep -l webhookUrl */src/main.js` vs `grep -c watchLabel`. All watch-mode Actors in the fleet now support a completion webhook — do not re-run that grep matrix expecting to find more targets; re-run it only after a *new* Actor ships with `watchLabel` but no `webhookUrl`.
- Same payload-shape discriminator held a third time: `hacker-news-scraper`'s `pushResult()` drops already-seen watch hits before the push loop (mirrors `trademark-search-scraper`), so `watchNewCount: pushed` with no change counter — not sam-gov's `pushed - changedCount` shape. Read the Actor's own pushResult/log logic before assuming either shape.
- Needed its own `scanned` counter too (had `fetched`, reset per query iteration, but no fleet-wide total) — same "add one, don't fake it" pattern as trademark-search-scraper cycle 576.

## Cycle 580 — a single Store search query can name the wrong competitor for 35 cycles
`apify-admin store "<query>"` is relevance-sorted, and relevance is text-similarity, not usage. On the UK-tenders niche the query `find a tender` put `nexgendata/uk-find-a-tender` (5 users, **0 u30d, 0 runs30d** — dead) at the top, while the niche's only listing with real 30-day usage, `ciel_labs/uk-government-tenders-contracts-finder` (14 users, 9 u30d), only appears under the sibling query `uk tenders`. Cycle 545 audited against the dead listing and recorded it as "the leader"; the real leader had already existed for 10 weeks. **Rule: every niche audit runs at least two sibling queries and ranks candidates by `u30d`, not by search position.** A competitor with 0 u30d is not a competitor — it is a corpse, and matching its feature set teaches you nothing.

## Cycle 580 — three copies of a Store description, and `publish` only syncs one
The Store `description`/`seoDescription` exist in `actors/<slug>/meta.json`, in `actors/<slug>/.actor/actor.json`, and live on the Apify record. `bin/apify-admin publish <slug> meta.json` pushes meta.json → live and leaves `.actor/actor.json` stale, which `bin/check-store-meta` then reports as drift with the **old** text labelled "local" — easy to misread as "the publish failed". It didn't; sync actor.json by hand and re-run. Separately, `publish` does not write the search index: `apify push --force` is still required, and `bin/check-store-index <slug>` must read 0 stale before any keyword/rank probe means anything (cycle 240 trap, re-confirmed live this cycle — index snapshot timestamp moved to exactly the new build's finish time).

## Cycle 581 (2026-09-21, opus-5) — the 4th "we're invisible" misread: a correction that lives only in LEARNINGS will be re-made by whoever runs the tool; plus the real discovery numbers and a new category lever

**The recurrence.** Cycle 580 ran `bin/store-visibility`, read `RESULT: still invisible to the public`, and built a strategic conclusion on it ("0 of 22 visible to anonymous buyers; the binding constraint is account-level discovery; niche audits are now low-yield"). That is the same wrong-surface error as cycles 1-20, 168 and 517 — the 4th instance, and cycle 518's own LEARNINGS entry predicted it by name ("if a fourth correction is ever needed, read this entry and cycles 168/452/517 in full"). Re-verified on the real surface: all 22 Actors are in Algolia `prod_PUBLIC_STORE` and retrievable anonymously, **8 of 22 top-20 on their primary query** (fec p1 `super pac`, trademark p4, court-records p5, sam-gov p5, scholarship p9, ats p13, uk-find-a-tender p18, nih p19).

**Root cause, and the reusable rule.** Cycle 518 did everything right except one thing: it wrote the correction into LEARNINGS and patched `bin/check-store-rank`, but left `bin/store-visibility`'s docstring asserting the blackout narrative and its stdout printing `still invisible to the public`. A future cycle reading a 62-cycle-old LEARNINGS file is a coin flip; a future cycle reading the tool's own output is a certainty. **When a finding invalidates a tool's premise, patch the TOOL — its docstring AND the strings it prints — in the same cycle. Prose corrections filed elsewhere do not stop the tool from lying.** Fixed here: SCOPE banner now prints ABOVE the table (where output is read, not below it), names `bin/store-rank` as the buyer-facing tool, and lists the four misreads so the next reader sees the history without going hunting.

**Corollary on where to put a warning:** a caveat printed *after* a result table is read after the reader has already formed a conclusion. Put it before.

**The real discovery picture (numbers worth keeping).** Search finds us; **category browse does not.** Algolia facet counts over the whole store (72,169 Actors): AUTOMATION 30,028 / DEVELOPER_TOOLS 23,034 / LEAD_GENERATION 22,519 / ECOMMERCE 13,922 / SOCIAL_MEDIA 11,091 / AI 9,176 / OTHER 7,987 / BUSINESS 7,242 / JOBS 6,320 / REAL_ESTATE 5,132 / SEO_TOOLS 4,478 / NEWS 3,870 / AGENTS 3,803 / VIDEOS 3,458 / INTEGRATIONS 3,098 / TRAVEL 2,564 / MCP_SERVERS 2,392 / MARKETING 2,043 / OPEN_SOURCE 994 / **EDUCATION 390 / FOR_CREATORS 247 / SPORTS 246 / GAMES 109** / DEVELOPER_EXAMPLES 7 / COVID_19 2. We had filed 13 of our 22 Actors in LEAD_GENERATION and are past rank 1000 in 6 of the 7 categories we occupy; the sole category we appear in at all is EDUCATION, at p206 of 390.

**New lever: `categories` is free, fully ours, and we had never once audited it.** It lives in `actors/<slug>/meta.json` (not `.actor/actor.json` — none of the 22 carry it there, so unlike `description` there is no third-copy sync trap), ships via `apify-admin publish`, and is live on the Algolia record. Category browse is ordered by `storePosition`, so predicted browse rank = count of listings in that category with a better `storePosition`. **Validate-before-ship worked here:** the model reproduces the one rank we can observe (`scholarship-scraper` predicted p206 of 390, measured p206), which turns the candidate list into a decision instead of a hope — `steam-reviews-scraper` is mis-filed in ECOMMERCE (13,922) when it is plainly a GAMES Actor (109), predicted ~p81/109. Bounded honestly: reachable-if-browsed, not featured.

**Process note that generalizes past this fleet:** two of this cycle's three findings came from *re-reading a prior cycle's conclusion against the tool that produced it*, not from new work. When a cycle hands you a big strategic claim, the cheapest high-value move is to check which command produced it and what that command actually measures.

## Cycle 582 — category browse is a third, separate Store surface, and its rank is exactly predictable

**Three surfaces, three tools, do not mix them up** (this confusion has now recurred 4 times through cycle 580, so it gets a permanent table):
| surface | what a buyer does | tool | mechanics |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/v2/store` REST | nothing — CLI/API only, **not buyer-facing** | `bin/store-visibility` | irrelevant to discovery |
| apify.com/store search box | types a query | `bin/store-rank` | Algolia `prod_PUBLIC_STORE`; title-match beats description-match, then `storePosition` |
| apify.com/store category browse | clicks a category in the sidebar | `bin/category-rank` (new) | same index, empty query + `categories` facet filter; order is **plain `storePosition` ascending** |

**Category-browse rank is computable in O(1) and the prediction is exact, not approximate.** Because browse order is nothing but `storePosition` ascending, an Actor's rank inside a category is `count(listings in category with storePosition < ours) + 1`, which is a single Algolia query with `hitsPerPage: 0` and `numericFilters: ["storePosition<N"]` — read `nbHits`, no paging, no 1000-hit cap. Verified 2-for-2 against the real ordered listing: `scholarship-scraper` predicted p206/390 in EDUCATION and measured p206; `steam-reviews-scraper` predicted p81/110 in GAMES and, after the category was actually shipped, measured p81. **Consequence: never ship a category edit to find out where it lands.** Predict first, ship only if the number justifies the slot.

**Category size varies by 4 orders of magnitude, and `categories` is a free field we control.** Measured over the full 72,179-listing store: AUTOMATION 30,026 / DEVELOPER_TOOLS 23,034 / LEAD_GENERATION 22,525 / ECOMMERCE 13,926 … down to EDUCATION 390 / SPORTS 250 / FOR_CREATORS 247 / **GAMES 110**. Moving `steam-reviews-scraper` from ECOMMERCE to GAMES moved it from **p14472 of 14809 to p81 of 110** for the cost of one `meta.json` edit and a rebuild. Unlike `storePosition` (Apify-computed from cumulative usage, unsettable) this is entirely ours.

**But size the honest ceiling before spending slots on it.** A good rank in a 110-item category makes you reachable by someone who browses that category to its bottom third; it is not featuring, and it does not touch search rank at all. It is also only available where the fit is *genuine* — of our 22 Actors only 4 have a small category they honestly belong to, because 13 are government-data Actors and the store has no small government category. The temptation to file an Actor somewhere small purely for the number is the wrong trade: quality score and user reviews are the ranking inputs that compound, and a conspicuously miscategorized listing in a 110-item category damages both.

**PLAYBOOK step 7's category list is stale — do not treat it as the vocabulary.** It omits GAMES, SPORTS, FOR_CREATORS, OPEN_SOURCE, MCP_SERVERS, VIDEOS, INTEGRATIONS, COVID_19, DEVELOPER_EXAMPLES. `GAMES` publishes fine (200). The live 25-value vocabulary is whatever `bin/category-rank --facets` prints; read it from the index, not from a note.

**`check-store-index` reporting "0 stale" does NOT mean a category edit has landed.** That tool only diffs `title`/`description`/`seoTitle`/`seoDescription`. For ~1-2 minutes after the force-build the facet query still served the old category set *and* the old facet count (GAMES read 109 with us absent, then 110 with us at p81) while `check-store-index` already read clean. Re-query the facet before concluding a category edit failed — the same "wait and re-measure" rule cycle 520 wrote for the `storePosition` 999999 sentinel.

## Cycle 583 (2026-09-21) — "does the filter actually filter?" is a distinct, productive probe class; USAspending's award-level date window is NOT a window
- **New probe class worth rotating through the fleet: filter fidelity.** For each documented filter input, run it live and assert every returned row actually satisfies it. This is different from every existing check (`check-field-fill` = is the field populated, `check-real-fields`/`check-code-fields` = does the field exist, `check-entities` = is the text clean). It found a real defect on its first use, on an Actor whose README was otherwise excellent. Method: `bin/varied-test <slug> '{filters...,"maxResults":10}' <the output fields the filters claim to constrain>` and read the columns.
- **Verified clean (filters honoured on 10/10 rows):** `nih-reporter-scraper` — `keyword`+`orgStates`+`fiscalYears`+`minAwardAmount`+`activityCodes`, then `agencyIcCodes`+`awardNoticeDateFrom/To`+`maxAwardAmount`+`activeOnly`. `federal-register-scraper` — `documentTypes`+`agencies`+`publicationDateFrom/To`, `cfrTitle`+`cfrPart`, `significantOnly`.
- **`federal-register-scraper` date window is inclusive on BOTH ends** (`publicationDateFrom=publicationDateTo=2026-08-19` returned exactly the 3 rows the wider window showed for that day). The `dateto-filter-silently-excludes-its-own-last-day` gotcha we have a blog post about does NOT apply to this Actor — don't assume it generalises.
- **A 0-row result is not automatically a bug — decompose before believing it.** `cfrTitle:40 + cfrPart:"52" + significantOnly` returned 0. Each filter alone returned rows, and the run log itself named the cause (the undeclared date window defaults to the last 90 days); widening to 2015-01-01 returned 5 rows. True negative, correctly explained to the user.
- **REAL DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED — `us-federal-awards-scraper` README FAQ was measurably false.** It claimed `startDate`/`endDate` "filter on the award's action date … `lastModifiedDate` is what actually falls inside your range". Measured (contracts, CA, NAICS 541512, ≥$1M, window 2024-01-01..2024-12-31): only **1 of 10** rows had `lastModifiedDate` inside the window; 9 were *later*. One matched row's period of performance was 2018-05-15..2023-09-30 and its 47 upstream transactions contain **no** 2024 action date at all.
- **The underlying upstream semantic, measured directly against `POST /api/v2/search/spending_by_award/` (so it is NOT our bug — the same filters reproduce it):** a **two-day** `time_period` (2024-03-01..2024-03-02) returns the *identical* top-5 awards as the full year 2024. Moving the window's **end** does change the result set (a 2026-09 window returns different awards); narrowing its **start** barely does. So USAspending's award-level `time_period` behaves as a coarse recency bound, not a window. Fixed the README FAQ + input table + both `input_schema` descriptions + the zero-match run-log hint to say exactly that, with the measurement inline (build 0.1.29, verified on the `latest`-tagged build's `readme` field per PLAYBOOK step 39).
- **Generalisable lesson**: our own FAQ prose about *upstream* filter semantics is unverified by every drift check we own (they all compare our code/schema/registry/README against each other, never against the source API's actual behaviour). When an FAQ answer asserts "field X is what falls inside your range", that is a testable claim — test it.

## Cycle 584 — filter-fidelity sweep, round 2 (grants-gov, sam-gov, eu-ted): 2nd real doc defect found, same class as cycle 583
- **REAL DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED — `eu-ted-tenders-scraper` documented CPV matching backwards on BOTH surfaces, and the README's own worked example was the counterexample.** The `input_schema` said "Exact 8-digit codes only"; the README table said a division-level code expands "per the official CPV hierarchy — use a fully-specified code (e.g. `72267000`) for an exact match". Measured live (publication window 2025-03-01..2025-03-31, 10 rows per run): `["72000000"]` → 10/10 rows carried some `72…` code but only **5/10** the literal one; `["72220000"]` → **5/10** literal; and the README's own "exact match" example `["72267000"]` → only **6/10** literal, because its children `72267100`/`72267200` match too. **TED matches the whole CPV subtree at every level; there is no exact-code mode.** Reproduced on a second division in the post-push smoke run (`["45000000"]` returned a row tagged only `45240000`/`45220000`/`45262300`), so it is the general rule, not a CPV-72 quirk. Fixed in 3 surfaces (schema description, README input-table row, new README FAQ with the measurements inline + the post-filter workaround), build 0.1.25, verified on the `latest` build's `readme`+`input`.
- **New sub-rule for this probe class: a filter can be 100% honoured and still be mis-documented.** Every row TED returned genuinely matched the filter *as TED defines it* — a naive "does every row satisfy the filter?" assertion on the literal code would have called this a BUG (5/10 fail) when the real defect was our prose. Assert against the *upstream's* semantics, then check whether our docs state those semantics; the finding is usually in the docs.
- **Corollary worth remembering: a "more specific" input is not necessarily an exact one.** Hierarchical code vocabularies (CPV, NAICS, CFDA, ICD) almost always match a subtree. Never document "use a longer code for an exact match" without measuring — you can only match exactly on a leaf, and users cannot tell leaves from parents by looking at the code.
- **Verified clean (every documented filter honoured on every row):** `grants-gov-scraper` — run A `oppStatuses`+`fundingInstruments`+`fundingCategories`+`postedFrom/To` (10/10), run B `minAwardAmount:500000`+`closeDateFrom/To` (10/10, `awardCeiling` ≥ 500000 and every `closeDate` inside the window, so the client-side amount filter and the enrich-forcing it documents both work). `sam-gov-opportunities-scraper` — `naicsCodes`+`states`+`noticeTypes`+`activeOnly`+`enrichDetail` (2/2 rows, a true negative on a genuinely narrow combination) and `states:["WY"]` alone (10/10 `placeOfPerformanceState` = WY, no nulls leaking through). `eu-ted-tenders-scraper` — `countries`+`minValue`+`onlyOpenDeadlines`+`minDaysUntilDeadline`+`publishedWithinDays` (10/10).

## Cycle 585 — filter-fidelity sweep, round 3 (clinicaltrials): 3rd real doc defect, and the 2nd member of a pattern — "upstream normalises an imprecise input value"
- **REAL DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED — `clinicaltrials-scraper` documented six date windows without ever saying that a date can be a MONTH.** ClinicalTrials.gov lets sponsors enter `YYYY-MM` with no day, and a month-precision value behaves as **the 1st of that month** inside `AREA[<field>]RANGE[from,to]`. Measured live (lung cancer, RECRUITING, PHASE2, 10-row cap): `primaryCompletionDateFrom/To = 2026-06-01..2026-06-04` — a four-day window — **returns** the trials whose `primaryCompletionDate` is the bare string `2026-06` (NCT05902988, NCT05913089); `2026-06-05..2026-06-25` returns **only** full-date rows and silently drops them. So "trials reading out in the second half of June" misses every June trial that never stated a day. Reproduced on a second field in the post-push smoke run (`studyStartDate` 2020-05-01..2020-05-03 on melanoma → 4/4 rows read bare `2020-05`), so it is the field-independent rule. Build 0.1.25; fixed on 4 surfaces (6 date `input_schema` descriptions, 3 README input-table rows, a new README FAQ with both measurements inline + the "start the window on the 1st and post-filter" workaround).
- **Which date fields are exposed and which are safe, measured not guessed** (one live 10-row recruiting sample): the three **sponsor-entered** dates are frequently month-only — `completionDate` 6/10, `startDate` 1/10, and `primaryCompletionDate` 4/10 on the separate 2026 run.
